claim: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) are ubiquitous in cultivated soils.
source: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) are ubiquitous in cultivated soils, forming symbiotic relationships with the roots of major crop species.
evidence: This is a general statement about AMF distribution that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: AMF form symbiotic relationships with the roots of major crop species.
source: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) are ubiquitous in cultivated soils, forming symbiotic relationships with the roots of major crop species.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature about AMF-plant interactions.

claim: Studies in controlled conditions have demonstrated the potential of AMF to enhance the growth of host plants.
source: Studies in controlled conditions have demonstrated the potential of AMF to enhance the growth of host plants.
evidence: This claim references previous research findings, implicitly citing the broader literature.

claim: It is difficult to estimate the actual benefit of AMF in the field because of the lack of suitable AMF-free controls.
source: However, it is difficult to estimate the actual benefit in the field, not least because of the lack of suitable AMF-free controls.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based claim about methodological challenges in field studies.

claim: A novel strategy using selective incorporation of AMF-resistance into a genetic mapping population can evaluate maize response to AMF.
source: Here we implement a novel strategy using the selective incorporation of AMF-resistance into a genetic mapping population to evaluate maize response to AMF.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: AMF account for about one-third of grain production in a medium input field.
source: We found AMF to account for about one-third of the grain production in a medium input field, as well as to affect the relative performance of different plant genotypes.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the field experiment reported in the study.

claim: AMF affect the relative performance of different plant genotypes.
source: We found AMF to account for about one-third of the grain production in a medium input field, as well as to affect the relative performance of different plant genotypes.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data showing genotype-by-AMF interactions.

claim: Characterization of the genetic architecture of host response indicated a trade-off between mycorrhizal dependence and benefit.
source: Characterization of the genetic architecture of the host response indicated a trade-off between mycorrhizal dependence and benefit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from QTL analysis and genetic data presented in the study.

claim: Several QTL are linked to host benefit from AMF.
source: We identified several QTL linked to host benefit, supporting the feasibility of breeding crops to maximize profit from symbiosis with AMF.
evidence: This is a direct result from the QTL mapping analysis.

claim: The identification of benefit QTL supports the feasibility of breeding crops to maximize profit from symbiosis with AMF.
source: We identified several QTL linked to host benefit, supporting the feasibility of breeding crops to maximize profit from symbiosis with AMF.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the QTL findings about breeding applications.

claim: There is a pressing need to develop sustainable agricultural systems that improve productivity whilst minimizing adverse environmental impacts.
source: There is a pressing need to develop sustainable agricultural systems that improve productivity whilst minimizing adverse environmental impacts (Lynch, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lynch, 2019.

claim: There is great interest in the potential contribution of arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis and other microbial mutualisms to sustainable agriculture.
source: In the face of this challenge, there is great interest in the potential contribution of arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) symbiosis and other microbial mutualisms (Sawers et al., 2008; Fester and Sawers, 2011; Bender et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: AMF occur broadly in cultivated soils.
source: AM fungi (AMF) occur broadly in cultivated soils, forming symbiotic relationships with the roots of major crop species and, indeed, many commercial 'biofertilizers' are available on the market (Faye et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a general statement about AMF distribution supported by citation.

claim: Many commercial 'biofertilizers' containing AMF are available on the market.
source: AM fungi (AMF) occur broadly in cultivated soils, forming symbiotic relationships with the roots of major crop species and, indeed, many commercial 'biofertilizers' are available on the market (Faye et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a factual statement about commercial products, supported by citation.

claim: The value of AM symbiosis in agriculture remains a matter of debate.
source: Nonetheless, the value of AM symbiosis in agriculture remains a matter of debate (Ryan and Graham, 2018; Rillig et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim about ongoing scientific debate is supported by citations.

claim: AMF enhance uptake of immobile soil nutrients, especially phosphorus.
source: Experimental studies under controlled conditions have demonstrated that AMF have much to offer host plants, including enhanced uptake of immobile soil nutrients (especially phosphorus) and water, and improved tolerance to a range of abiotic and biotic stresses (Borowicz, 2001; Chandrasekaran et al., 2014; Augé et al., 2015; Chiu and Paszkowski, 2019).
evidence: This is a well-documented benefit of AMF supported by multiple citations.

claim: AMF enhance water uptake in host plants.
source: Experimental studies under controlled conditions have demonstrated that AMF have much to offer host plants, including enhanced uptake of immobile soil nutrients (especially phosphorus) and water, and improved tolerance to a range of abiotic and biotic stresses (Borowicz, 2001; Chandrasekaran et al., 2014; Augé et al., 2015; Chiu and Paszkowski, 2019).
evidence: This benefit is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: AMF improve host plant tolerance to a range of abiotic and biotic stresses.
source: Experimental studies under controlled conditions have demonstrated that AMF have much to offer host plants, including enhanced uptake of immobile soil nutrients (especially phosphorus) and water, and improved tolerance to a range of abiotic and biotic stresses (Borowicz, 2001; Chandrasekaran et al., 2014; Augé et al., 2015; Chiu and Paszkowski, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: AMF contribute important ecosystem services.
source: AMF also contribute important ecosystem services (van der Heijden et al., 2015), including promoting soil aggregation (Rillig and Mummey, 2006) and reducing nutrient loss through leaching and emission (Bender et al., 2014; Cavagnaro et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van der Heijden et al., 2015.

claim: AMF promote soil aggregation.
source: AMF also contribute important ecosystem services (van der Heijden et al., 2015), including promoting soil aggregation (Rillig and Mummey, 2006) and reducing nutrient loss through leaching and emission (Bender et al., 2014; Cavagnaro et al., 2015).
evidence: This specific ecosystem service is supported by citation to Rillig and Mummey, 2006.

claim: AMF reduce nutrient loss through leaching and emission.
source: AMF also contribute important ecosystem services (van der Heijden et al., 2015), including promoting soil aggregation (Rillig and Mummey, 2006) and reducing nutrient loss through leaching and emission (Bender et al., 2014; Cavagnaro et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bender et al., 2014 and Cavagnaro et al., 2015.

claim: Efforts to integrate AMF into agricultural practice are hampered by the difficulty of evaluating host response in the field and the lack of appropriate AMF free controls.
source: However, efforts to integrate AMF into agricultural practice are hampered by the difficulty of evaluating host response in the field and the lack of appropriate AMF free controls.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based claim about methodological challenges.

claim: When exogenous fungal inoculum is applied to a field, it is difficult to gauge its effectiveness with respect to the native fungal community.
source: When exogenous fungal inoculum is applied to a field, it is difficult to gauge its effectiveness with respect to the native fungal community; when looking to evaluate the impact of the native AMF community under any given agronomic scenario, there is no easy way to estimate what the baseline performance of plants would be if AMF were absent.
evidence: This is an inference about experimental challenges in field studies.

claim: There is no easy way to estimate what the baseline performance of plants would be if AMF were absent when evaluating the impact of the native AMF community.
source: When exogenous fungal inoculum is applied to a field, it is difficult to gauge its effectiveness with respect to the native fungal community; when looking to evaluate the impact of the native AMF community under any given agronomic scenario, there is no easy way to estimate what the baseline performance of plants would be if AMF were absent.
evidence: This is an inference about methodological limitations.

claim: Chemical treatments and mechanical barriers can be implemented at a small scale to create AMF-free controls but are not practical for use in larger genetic studies or trials.
source: Although experimental designs using chemical treatments and/or mechanical barriers can be implemented at a small scale, they are not practical for use in larger genetic studies or trials.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of existing methods.

claim: The incorporation of plant mycorrhizal mutants in the design of experiments can address difficulties in studying AM symbiosis in the field.
source: To address these difficulties, we propose the incorporation of plant mycorrhizal mutants in the design of experiments to study AM symbiosis in the field.
evidence: This is a proposed methodological solution based on the study's approach.

claim: AM symbiosis dates back over 450 million years.
source: AM symbiosis dates back over 450 million years (Strullu-Derrien et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a factual claim about evolutionary history supported by citation.

claim: Agriculture is a recent development compared to AM symbiosis.
source: By contrast, agriculture is a recent development.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on established knowledge.

claim: Modern breeding efforts have focused on maximizing yield under homogeneous environments with large quantities of synthetic inputs.
source: Modern breeding efforts have focused on maximizing yield under homogeneous environments with large quantities of synthetic inputs, and it is not clear how the breeding process has impacted the AM symbiosis (discussed in Sawers et al., 2008; Sawers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a general statement about breeding practices supported by citations.

claim: It is not clear how the breeding process has impacted the AM symbiosis.
source: Modern breeding efforts have focused on maximizing yield under homogeneous environments with large quantities of synthetic inputs, and it is not clear how the breeding process has impacted the AM symbiosis (discussed in Sawers et al., 2008; Sawers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about uncertainty in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Modern crop varieties retain the molecular machinery necessary for symbiotic establishment.
source: Modern crop varieties retain the molecular machinery necessary for symbiotic establishment and are colonized to high levels in controlled experiments (e.g. Gutjahr et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental evidence.

claim: Modern crop varieties are colonized to high levels by AMF in controlled experiments.
source: Modern crop varieties retain the molecular machinery necessary for symbiotic establishment and are colonized to high levels in controlled experiments (e.g. Gutjahr et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: Molecular genetic analyses in Medicago truncatula and Lotus japonicus have identified a series of plant-encoded receptor and signal-transduction components necessary for AM symbiosis.
source: Elegant molecular genetic analyses, largely conducted in Medicago truncatula and Lotus japonicus, have identified a series of plant-encoded receptor and signal-transduction components necessary for AM symbiosis and, in relevant host plants, for interaction with nodule-forming rhizobia.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from molecular genetic studies.

claim: The plant-encoded receptor and signal-transduction components necessary for AM symbiosis are also necessary for interaction with nodule-forming rhizobia in relevant host plants.
source: Elegant molecular genetic analyses, largely conducted in Medicago truncatula and Lotus japonicus, have identified a series of plant-encoded receptor and signal-transduction components necessary for AM symbiosis and, in relevant host plants, for interaction with nodule-forming rhizobia.
evidence: This is established knowledge from molecular genetic studies.

claim: Fungal signals are perceived by a partially-characterized suite of host LysM receptor kinases acting in combination with the SYMRK (DMI2) receptor.
source: Fungal signals are perceived by a partially-characterized suite of host LysM receptor kinases, acting in combination with the SYMRK (DMI2) receptor.
evidence: This describes the molecular mechanism based on established research, supported by the subsequent citation.

claim: Signal perception triggers cellular calcium spiking events through the action of the nuclear ion-channels CASTOR and POLLUX (DMI1).
source: Signal perception triggers cellular calcium spiking events, through the action of the nuclear ion-channels CASTOR and POLLUX (DMI1), resulting in the activation of downstream genes via the action of the CCaMK (DMI3) and CYCLOPS (IPD3) proteins (Parniske, 2008; Zipfel and Oldroyd, 2017).
evidence: This describes the signaling pathway supported by citations.

claim: Calcium spiking results in the activation of downstream genes via the action of the CCaMK (DMI3) and CYCLOPS (IPD3) proteins.
source: Signal perception triggers cellular calcium spiking events, through the action of the nuclear ion-channels CASTOR and POLLUX (DMI1), resulting in the activation of downstream genes via the action of the CCaMK (DMI3) and CYCLOPS (IPD3) proteins (Parniske, 2008; Zipfel and Oldroyd, 2017).
evidence: This describes the signaling pathway supported by citations.

claim: There is little genetic redundancy in the common symbiotic signaling pathway (CSSP).
source: Notwithstanding the great antiquity of AM symbiosis, there is little genetic redundancy in this common symbiotic signaling pathway (CSSP) and single host gene mutations are sufficient to block symbiotic interaction (e.g. Charpentier et al., 2008; Gutjahr et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: Single host gene mutations in the CSSP are sufficient to block symbiotic interaction.
source: Notwithstanding the great antiquity of AM symbiosis, there is little genetic redundancy in this common symbiotic signaling pathway (CSSP) and single host gene mutations are sufficient to block symbiotic interaction (e.g. Charpentier et al., 2008; Gutjahr et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental evidence.

claim: Among major cereal crops, CSSP mutations have only been reported in rice.
source: Among the major cereal crops, CSSP mutations have only been reported in rice (Charpentier et al., 2008; Gutjahr et al., 2008), although the genes themselves can be unambiguously identified in the genomes of maize, wheat, and sorghum, amongst others (Chiu and Paszkowski, 2020).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the literature supported by citations.

claim: CSSP genes can be unambiguously identified in the genomes of maize, wheat, and sorghum.
source: Among the major cereal crops, CSSP mutations have only been reported in rice (Charpentier et al., 2008; Gutjahr et al., 2008), although the genes themselves can be unambiguously identified in the genomes of maize, wheat, and sorghum, amongst others (Chiu and Paszkowski, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to genomic analysis.

claim: The CSSP is essential for plant interaction with AMF.
source: The CSSP is essential for plant interaction with AMF but does not appear to be a major point of regulation of AM symbiosis with respect to either host development or environment.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from genetic studies.

claim: The CSSP does not appear to be a major point of regulation of AM symbiosis with respect to either host development or environment.
source: The CSSP is essential for plant interaction with AMF but does not appear to be a major point of regulation of AM symbiosis with respect to either host development or environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature and observations.

claim: There are many reports of intra-specific differences in the impact AM symbiosis has on the plant host.
source: There are, however, many reports of intra-specific differences in the impact AM symbiosis has on the plant host (e.g. Kaeppler et al., 2000; Mascher et al., 2014; Diedhiou et al., 2016; Sawers et al., 2017; Watts‐Williams et al., 2019; Pawlowski et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: A variant of the OsCERK1 LysM receptor kinase present in Oryza rufipogon has been linked to greater colonization by AMF and enhanced host response.
source: In the case of rice, a variant of the OsCERK1 LysM receptor kinase present in the wild progenitor species Oryza rufipogon has been linked to greater colonization by AMF and enhanced host response, although this variant was not found to be segregating in the agronomically important japonica group (Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2020.

claim: The OsCERK1 variant linked to greater AMF colonization was not found to be segregating in the agronomically important japonica rice group.
source: In the case of rice, a variant of the OsCERK1 LysM receptor kinase present in the wild progenitor species Oryza rufipogon has been linked to greater colonization by AMF and enhanced host response, although this variant was not found to be segregating in the agronomically important japonica group (Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2020.

claim: The mechanistic basis of host response variation remains largely uncharacterized apart from the OsCERK1 result in rice.
source: Apart from this interesting result, the mechanistic basis of host response variation remains largely uncharacterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Host response to AMF is typically defined as the difference between mycorrhizal and non-mycorrhizal plants, expressed in either absolute or relative terms.
source: Typically, host response to AMF is defined as the difference between mycorrhizal and non-mycorrhizal plants, expressed in either absolute or relative terms (Janos, 2007).
evidence: This is a definition from the literature supported by citation.

claim: Dependence is the capacity of a given variety to perform in the absence of AMF.
source: We further differentiate dependence, the capacity of a given variety to perform in the absence of AMF, and benefit, the degree to which a plant host profits from the association (discussed in Janos, 2007; Sawers et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Benefit is the degree to which a plant host profits from the association with AMF.
source: We further differentiate dependence, the capacity of a given variety to perform in the absence of AMF, and benefit, the degree to which a plant host profits from the association (discussed in Janos, 2007; Sawers et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Variation in host response confounds differences in both dependence and benefit.
source: Importantly, variation in host response confounds differences in both dependence and benefit, with benefit being of the greater agronomic interest (Hetrick et al., 1992; Diedhiou et al., 2016; Sawers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of host response, supported by citations.

claim: Benefit is of greater agronomic interest than dependence.
source: Importantly, variation in host response confounds differences in both dependence and benefit, with benefit being of the greater agronomic interest (Hetrick et al., 1992; Diedhiou et al., 2016; Sawers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a value judgment about agronomic priorities, supported by citations.

claim: The study evaluates the impact of AMF in a cultivated field using concepts of genotype x environment interaction (GEI), considering mycorrhizal and non-mycorrhizal growth as two distinct 'environments'.
source: In this study we evaluate the impact of AMF in a cultivated field and distinguish dependence and benefit using the concepts of genotype x environment interaction (GEI; Des Marais and Juenger, 2010), considering mycorrhizal and non-mycorrhizal growth as two distinct 'environments'.
evidence: This describes the conceptual framework of the study, supported by citation.

claim: A mutation in the CSSP gene Castor was selectively incorporated into a bi-parental maize population for quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping to establish a non-mycorrhizal condition in the field.
source: To establish a non-mycorrhizal condition in the field, we selectively incorporated a mutation in the CSSP gene Castor into a bi-parental maize population for quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: The mapping population contained both AMF susceptible (AMF-S) and resistant (AMF-R) families.
source: The resulting population contained both AMF susceptible (AMF-S) and resistant (AMF-R) families (we use resistance here to denote an inability to from AM symbiosis due to host incompatibility), allowing us to map the interaction between plant trait QTL and AM symbiosis.
evidence: This describes the composition of the experimental population.

claim: Resistance to AMF denotes an inability to form AM symbiosis due to host incompatibility.
source: The resulting population contained both AMF susceptible (AMF-S) and resistant (AMF-R) families (we use resistance here to denote an inability to from AM symbiosis due to host incompatibility), allowing us to map the interaction between plant trait QTL and AM symbiosis.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors.

claim: The study reports a significant contribution of AM symbiosis in the field experiment.
source: We report a significant contribution of AM symbiosis in our field experiment, along with an empirical demonstration of dependence and benefit variation, and evidence of a trade-off between the two.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the experimental data.

claim: The study provides an empirical demonstration of dependence and benefit variation.
source: We report a significant contribution of AM symbiosis in our field experiment, along with an empirical demonstration of dependence and benefit variation, and evidence of a trade-off between the two.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the data analysis.

claim: There is evidence of a trade-off between mycorrhizal dependence and benefit.
source: We report a significant contribution of AM symbiosis in our field experiment, along with an empirical demonstration of dependence and benefit variation, and evidence of a trade-off between the two.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: Maize orthologs of CASTOR and POLLUX (DMI1) were identified in var. B73.
source: To generate AMF-resistant maize varieties for use in field experiments, we identified maize (var. B73) orthologs of the common-symbiosis genes CASTOR and POLLUX (DMI1) (Parniske, 2008; www.maizegdb.org).
evidence: This describes a bioinformatics analysis performed in the study.

claim: CASTOR and POLLUX are single copy genes in maize.
source: As in rice, CASTOR and POLLUX were found to be single copy genes in maize, and designated ZmCastor (GRMZM2G099160; Zm00001d012863; chromosome 5, 1 Mb) and ZmPollux (GRMZM2G110897; Zm00001d042694; chromosome 3, 177 Mb).
evidence: This is a finding from genomic analysis.

claim: ZmCastor is located on chromosome 5 at 1 Mb.
source: As in rice, CASTOR and POLLUX were found to be single copy genes in maize, and designated ZmCastor (GRMZM2G099160; Zm00001d012863; chromosome 5, 1 Mb) and ZmPollux (GRMZM2G110897; Zm00001d042694; chromosome 3, 177 Mb).
evidence: This is genomic location information from database analysis.

claim: ZmPollux is located on chromosome 3 at 177 Mb.
source: As in rice, CASTOR and POLLUX were found to be single copy genes in maize, and designated ZmCastor (GRMZM2G099160; Zm00001d012863; chromosome 5, 1 Mb) and ZmPollux (GRMZM2G110897; Zm00001d042694; chromosome 3, 177 Mb).
evidence: This is genomic location information from database analysis.

claim: Two Mutator (Mu) transposon insertions in the Castor gene were identified in publicly available genetic resources.
source: We searched publicly available genetic resources (McCarty et al., 2005) and identified two Mutator (Mu) transposon insertions in the Castor gene, castor-1 (44 bp upstream of the translational start site) and castor-2 (39 bp downstream of the translational start site. Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the identification of mutant alleles from a genetic resource, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The castor-1 insertion is located 44 bp upstream of the translational start site.
source: We searched publicly available genetic resources (McCarty et al., 2005) and identified two Mutator (Mu) transposon insertions in the Castor gene, castor-1 (44 bp upstream of the translational start site) and castor-2 (39 bp downstream of the translational start site. Figure 1A).
evidence: This is molecular characterization data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The castor-2 insertion is located 39 bp downstream of the translational start site.
source: We searched publicly available genetic resources (McCarty et al., 2005) and identified two Mutator (Mu) transposon insertions in the Castor gene, castor-1 (44 bp upstream of the translational start site) and castor-2 (39 bp downstream of the translational start site. Figure 1A).
evidence: This is molecular characterization data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Following controlled inoculation with AMF, castor-1 plants showed fungal colonization.
source: Following controlled inoculation with AMF, we saw fungal colonization of castor-1 plants but found castor-2 plants to be free from root-internal fungal structures, reflecting the different sites of transposon insertion in the two alleles (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is experimental data from inoculation assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Following controlled inoculation with AMF, castor-2 plants were free from root-internal fungal structures.
source: Following controlled inoculation with AMF, we saw fungal colonization of castor-1 plants but found castor-2 plants to be free from root-internal fungal structures, reflecting the different sites of transposon insertion in the two alleles (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is experimental data from inoculation assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The difference in colonization between castor-1 and castor-2 reflects the different sites of transposon insertion in the two alleles.
source: Following controlled inoculation with AMF, we saw fungal colonization of castor-1 plants but found castor-2 plants to be free from root-internal fungal structures, reflecting the different sites of transposon insertion in the two alleles (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular and phenotypic data.

claim: The Castor transcript is disrupted in castor-2 mutants.
source: We advanced castor-2 (hereafter, castor) mutants for more detailed quantitative characterization, finding the transcript to be disrupted in the mutants and confirming the absence of fungal colonization following inoculation with either crude (sand-pot produced) or plate-cultured (in vitro produced) inoculum (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is molecular data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: castor-2 mutants show absence of fungal colonization following inoculation with crude (sand-pot produced) inoculum.
source: We advanced castor-2 (hereafter, castor) mutants for more detailed quantitative characterization, finding the transcript to be disrupted in the mutants and confirming the absence of fungal colonization following inoculation with either crude (sand-pot produced) or plate-cultured (in vitro produced) inoculum (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is experimental data from inoculation assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: castor-2 mutants show absence of fungal colonization following inoculation with plate-cultured (in vitro produced) inoculum.
source: We advanced castor-2 (hereafter, castor) mutants for more detailed quantitative characterization, finding the transcript to be disrupted in the mutants and confirming the absence of fungal colonization following inoculation with either crude (sand-pot produced) or plate-cultured (in vitro produced) inoculum (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is experimental data from inoculation assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The castor mutation does not result in gross defects in plant development under high-nutrient field conditions.
source: We confirmed that resistance to AMF was stable in the field (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and that under high-nutrient field conditions the castor mutation did not result in any gross defects in plant development or show marked pleiotropic effects beyond the block in mycorrhizal colonization (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is experimental data from field trials shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Under high-nutrient field conditions, the castor mutation does not show marked pleiotropic effects beyond the block in mycorrhizal colonization.
source: We confirmed that resistance to AMF was stable in the field (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and that under high-nutrient field conditions the castor mutation did not result in any gross defects in plant development or show marked pleiotropic effects beyond the block in mycorrhizal colonization (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is experimental data from field trials shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The observations do not exclude more subtle, or environmentally dependent, pleiotropy of the castor mutation.
source: We note that our observations do not exclude more subtle, or environmentally dependent, pleiotropy.
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the data.

claim: The F2:3 population was evaluated in a replicated trial under rain-fed, medium-input conditions at Ameca, Mexico.
source: To characterize the genetic architecture of host response to AMF in the field, we evaluated the 73 AMF-S and 64 AMF-R families in a replicated trial under rain-fed, medium-input, conditions (Ameca, Mexico. Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3; three replicates, using three-row plots at 15 individuals per row).
evidence: This describes the field trial design and location.

claim: The agronomic scenario was representative of medium scale, subtropical production.
source: We chose an agronomic scenario that was representative of medium scale, subtropical production, and conditions under which we might expect AMF to be important.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the experimental conditions.

claim: AMF-R families tended to exhibit mild-chlorosis compared to AMF-S families.
source: Overall, AMF-R families tended to exhibit mild-chlorosis (Figure 2B) and produce visibly poorer ears than AMF-S families (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is an observation from field phenotyping shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AMF-R families produce visibly poorer ears than AMF-S families.
source: Overall, AMF-R families tended to exhibit mild-chlorosis (Figure 2B) and produce visibly poorer ears than AMF-S families (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is an observation from field phenotyping shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: Roots of AMF-S families showed clear colonization by AMF.
source: We inspected the roots of a random sampling of plants, finding clear colonization by AMF of AMF-S families and an absence of AM fungal structures in AMF-R families.
evidence: This is observational data from root inspection.

claim: Roots of AMF-R families showed an absence of AM fungal structures.
source: We inspected the roots of a random sampling of plants, finding clear colonization by AMF of AMF-S families and an absence of AM fungal structures in AMF-R families.
evidence: This is observational data from root inspection.

claim: Ten of fifteen traits differed significantly between AMF-S and AMF-R families.
source: We collected fifteen phenological and morphological traits and yield-components (Figure 2E–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Supplementary file 1). Ten of fifteen traits differed significantly between AMF-S and AMF-R families, corresponding to positive host responses ranging from 3% to 51% (Table 1; positive defined here as greater values of growth traits and yield components or accelerated/more synchronous flowering).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the phenotypic data shown in Table 1 and figures.

claim: Positive host responses ranged from 3% to 51%.
source: Ten of fifteen traits differed significantly between AMF-S and AMF-R families, corresponding to positive host responses ranging from 3% to 51% (Table 1; positive defined here as greater values of growth traits and yield components or accelerated/more synchronous flowering).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary from the data analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: AMF-R families were reduced in stature compared to AMF-S families.
source: AMF-R families were reduced in stature and delayed in silking (female flowering), resulting in an extension of anthesis (male flowering)-silking interval (ASI; Figure 2E,F; Supplementary file 1) - a classic symptom of abiotic stress in maize.
evidence: This is phenotypic data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: AMF-R families were delayed in silking (female flowering) compared to AMF-S families.
source: AMF-R families were reduced in stature and delayed in silking (female flowering), resulting in an extension of anthesis (male flowering)-silking interval (ASI; Figure 2E,F; Supplementary file 1) - a classic symptom of abiotic stress in maize.
evidence: This is phenotypic data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: AMF-R families showed an extension of anthesis-silking interval (ASI).
source: AMF-R families were reduced in stature and delayed in silking (female flowering), resulting in an extension of anthesis (male flowering)-silking interval (ASI; Figure 2E,F; Supplementary file 1) - a classic symptom of abiotic stress in maize.
evidence: This is phenotypic data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Extension of anthesis-silking interval is a classic symptom of abiotic stress in maize.
source: AMF-R families were reduced in stature and delayed in silking (female flowering), resulting in an extension of anthesis (male flowering)-silking interval (ASI; Figure 2E,F; Supplementary file 1) - a classic symptom of abiotic stress in maize.
evidence: This is established knowledge about maize stress responses.

claim: Ear size was reduced in AMF-R families compared to AMF-S families.
source: Ear size was reduced in AMF-R families, along with ear and total kernel weight (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is phenotypic data shown in Table 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Ear weight was reduced in AMF-R families compared to AMF-S families.
source: Ear size was reduced in AMF-R families, along with ear and total kernel weight (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is phenotypic data shown in Table 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Total kernel weight was reduced in AMF-R families compared to AMF-S families.
source: Ear size was reduced in AMF-R families, along with ear and total kernel weight (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is phenotypic data shown in Table 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Individual kernels were not significantly different in weight between AMF-S and AMF-R families.
source: Individual kernels were not significantly different in weight or size between AMF-S and AMF-R families (Figure 2G; Table 1).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of phenotypic data shown in Figure 2G and Table 1.

claim: Individual kernels were not significantly different in size between AMF-S and AMF-R families.
source: Individual kernels were not significantly different in weight or size between AMF-S and AMF-R families (Figure 2G; Table 1).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of phenotypic data shown in Figure 2G and Table 1.

claim: The total number of kernels per ear was reduced in AMF-R families.
source: However, the total number of kernels per ear was reduced in AMF-R families (Figure 2H; Table 1), indicative of poor seed set, a possible consequence of increased ASI.
evidence: This is phenotypic data shown in Figure 2H and Table 1.

claim: Reduced kernel number per ear is indicative of poor seed set.
source: However, the total number of kernels per ear was reduced in AMF-R families (Figure 2H; Table 1), indicative of poor seed set, a possible consequence of increased ASI.
evidence: This is an inference based on agronomic knowledge.

claim: Poor seed set is a possible consequence of increased ASI.
source: However, the total number of kernels per ear was reduced in AMF-R families (Figure 2H; Table 1), indicative of poor seed set, a possible consequence of increased ASI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between flowering synchrony and seed set.

claim: 28 QTLs were identified in the study.
source: We identified 28 QTLs, of which 21 showed evidence of AMF × QTL interaction (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the QTL mapping analysis shown in Figure 3A and Table 1.

claim: 21 of the 28 QTLs showed evidence of AMF × QTL interaction.
source: We identified 28 QTLs, of which 21 showed evidence of AMF × QTL interaction (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the QTL mapping analysis shown in Figure 3A and Table 1.

claim: For plant height, ear weight and total kernel weight, the combination of AMF and AMF x QTL effects explained more than half of the total genetic variance.
source: For plant height, ear weight and total kernel weight, the combination of AMF and AMF x QTL effects explained more than half of the total genetic variance (based on an estimation of broad-sense heritability, H2), and over a quarter of the total phenotypic variance (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from variance partitioning analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For plant height, ear weight and total kernel weight, the combination of AMF and AMF x QTL effects explained over a quarter of the total phenotypic variance.
source: For plant height, ear weight and total kernel weight, the combination of AMF and AMF x QTL effects explained more than half of the total genetic variance (based on an estimation of broad-sense heritability, H2), and over a quarter of the total phenotypic variance (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from variance partitioning analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The identification of significant AMF × QTL effects reveals heritable differences in the response to AMF between the CML312 and W22 parents.
source: The identification of significant AMF × QTL effects reveals heritable differences in the response to AMF between the CML312 and W22 parents.
evidence: This is an inference from the QTL mapping results.

claim: For 12 of the 17 QTLs showing significant interaction, the effect was conditional - expressed predominantly in either the AMF-S or AMF-R families, but not in both.
source: Having identified significant AMF × QTL interaction, we distinguished dependence and benefit by inspecting QTL effects separately in AMF-S and AMF-R families (Figure 4—source data 1). For 12 of the 17 QTLs showing significant interaction, the effect was conditional - that is expressed predominantly in either the AMF-S or AMF-R families, but not in both (Figures 3A and 4; Table 1; Des Marais and Juenger, 2010).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing QTL effects separately in the two subpopulations.

claim: Conditional QTLs expressed specifically in the AMF-R families represent variation in dependence.
source: We considered conditional QTLs expressed specifically in the AMF-R families to represent variation in dependence.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the QTL patterns.

claim: Conditional QTLs expressed specifically in the AMF-S families represent variation in benefit.
source: Conversely, we considered conditional QTLs expressed specifically in the AMF-S families to be variation in benefit (Figures 3 and 4; Table 1).
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the QTL patterns.

claim: A region on the long arm of chromosome one is linked to ear-traits.
source: Two regions of the genome were associated with multiple QTLs, suggesting a shared mechanistic basis: a region on the long arm of chromosome (chr) one linked to ear-traits and a region on chr four linked to plant height and flowering time (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from QTL mapping shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A region on chromosome four is linked to plant height and flowering time.
source: Two regions of the genome were associated with multiple QTLs, suggesting a shared mechanistic basis: a region on the long arm of chromosome (chr) one linked to ear-traits and a region on chr four linked to plant height and flowering time (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from QTL mapping shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The co-localization of multiple QTLs in two genomic regions suggests a shared mechanistic basis.
source: Two regions of the genome were associated with multiple QTLs, suggesting a shared mechanistic basis: a region on the long arm of chromosome (chr) one linked to ear-traits and a region on chr four linked to plant height and flowering time (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference from the QTL mapping results.

claim: Several QTLs showed antagonistic pleiotropy where the effect was expressed in both AMF-S and AMF-R families but with a change of sign.
source: Several QTLs showed more extreme QTL × AMF in which the effect was expressed in both AMF-S and AMF-R families, but with a change of sign (i.e. a 'swap' in the relative performance of the parental alleles) - a condition described as antagonistic pleiotropy (Figure 4—figure supplements 1, Figure 5A; Des Marais and Juenger, 2010).
evidence: This is a result from QTL effect analysis shown in figures.

claim: Under antagonistic pleiotropy, the superior allele in mycorrhizal plants is detrimental to performance in the absence of mycorrhiza, and vice versa.
source: Under this scenario, the superior allele in mycorrhizal plants is detrimental to performance in the absence of mycorrhiza, and vice versa, providing evidence for a trade-off at the single-locus level.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the antagonistic pleiotropy pattern.

claim: Antagonistic pleiotropy provides evidence for a trade-off at the single-locus level.
source: Under this scenario, the superior allele in mycorrhizal plants is detrimental to performance in the absence of mycorrhiza, and vice versa, providing evidence for a trade-off at the single-locus level.
evidence: This is an inference from the QTL effect patterns.

claim: Several QTLs associated with key yield components showed antagonistic pleiotropy.
source: Significantly, several QTLs associated with key yield components showed antagonistic pleiotropy (Figure 3, Figure 4—source data 1, Figure 5B, C; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from QTL analysis shown in figures and tables.

claim: There is evidence of rank change in genotype performance with respect to presence or absence of AMF.
source: We observed analogous 'rank changing' effects at the level of the whole genotype. Although our mapping design did not permit direct evaluation of the same families as both AMF-S and AMF-R, we could fit QTL models to all genotypes across both levels of AMF. The resulting estimates showed evidence of rank change with respect to performance with or without AMF (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a result from QTL model fitting shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Whole-genome predictions aligned well with the observed values of their training sets.
source: Whole-genome predictions aligned well with the observed values of their training sets, although they did not capture the extreme observed values (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a result from genomic prediction analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Whole-genome predictions did not capture the extreme observed values.
source: Whole-genome predictions aligned well with the observed values of their training sets, although they did not capture the extreme observed values (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an observation from genomic prediction analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Genotypes associated with the highest values of major yield components in one AMF condition were unexceptional or poor in the other condition.
source: Comparison of the two models indicated that genotypes associated with the highest values of the major yield components in one condition were unexceptional or poor in the other (Figure 5F), indicating a trade-off between dependence and benefit.
evidence: This is a result from comparing genomic predictions shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The comparison of genomic prediction models indicates a trade-off between dependence and benefit.
source: Comparison of the two models indicated that genotypes associated with the highest values of the major yield components in one condition were unexceptional or poor in the other (Figure 5F), indicating a trade-off between dependence and benefit.
evidence: This is an inference from the genomic prediction results shown in Figure 5F.

claim: AM symbiosis makes a significant contribution to maize performance in a medium-input, rain fed, subtropical field.
source: We have presented evidence that AM symbiosis makes a significant contribution to maize performance in a medium-input, rain fed, subtropical field.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the field experiment data.

claim: Colonization by AMF would contribute approximately 2 tonnes/ha to a total yield of approximately 5.5 tonnes/ha in a field planted at 80,000 plants/ha.
source: Extrapolating our observations to a cultivated field planted at 80,000 plants/ha (typical in the locality of the trial site), we estimate that colonization by AMF would contribute ~2 tonnes/ha to a total yield of ~5.5 tonnes/ha.
evidence: This is an extrapolation from the experimental data to a typical field scenario.

claim: The estimate of AMF contribution to yield is a rough figure to be treated with caution.
source: Although a rough figure to be treated with caution, this estimate serves to provide an indication of the importance of AMF, and is consistent with the previous evaluation of an inbred mutant line that linked the loss of mycorrhizal phosphate uptake with a 15% reduction in ear-weight (Willmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the yield estimate.

claim: The estimate of AMF contribution is consistent with a previous evaluation that linked loss of mycorrhizal phosphate uptake with a 15% reduction in ear-weight.
source: Although a rough figure to be treated with caution, this estimate serves to provide an indication of the importance of AMF, and is consistent with the previous evaluation of an inbred mutant line that linked the loss of mycorrhizal phosphate uptake with a 15% reduction in ear-weight (Willmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This compares the current findings to previous work, supported by citation.

claim: The study evaluated only one location in a single season.
source: We have only evaluated one location, collecting data in a single season.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope of the study.

claim: It will be important to explore the stability of the mycorrhizal effect in subsequent years and in different locations, under a range of management practices.
source: It will be important to explore the stability of the mycorrhizal effect in subsequent years and in different locations, under a range of management practices.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Mycorrhiza will likely be more significant in more stressful environments.
source: We can hypothesize that mycorrhiza will be more significant in more stressful environments (e.g. Sawers et al., 2017; O'Brien et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Greater quantitative characterization is needed to obtain a more complete picture of the role of AM symbiosis in agriculture across the full range of agronomic scenarios.
source: Beyond such broad generalizations, greater quantitative characterization is needed to obtain a more complete picture of the role of AM symbiosis in agriculture , across the full range of agronomic scenarios, from smallholder plot to high-input intensive farm.
evidence: This is a statement about research needs.

claim: The approach described can be used to evaluate the functional impact of practices aimed at promoting or enriching soil health.
source: The approach we describe here can also be used to evaluate the functional impact of practices aimed at promoting or enriching soil health, including the overall 'organic package' or specific interventions such as reduced tillage or application of exogenous AMF or other microbes.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the methodology.

claim: Inbred maize varieties consistently show a positive response to AMF when grown under low to moderate nutrient availability.
source: Inbred maize varieties consistently show a positive response to AMF when grown under low to moderate nutrient availability (e.g. Kaeppler et al., 2000; Sawers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a general statement about maize-AMF interactions supported by citations.

claim: In other crop species, the impact of AMF is more variable, falling along a continuum from mutualism to parasitism.
source: In other crop species, the impact of AMF is more variable, falling along a continuum from mutualism to parasitism (Johnson et al., 1997; Wen et al., 2019; Bergmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a general statement about AMF effects in crops supported by citations.

claim: In sorghum, host response to AMF varies from positive to negative depending on both the plant variety and the AMF species.
source: In sorghum, a close relative of maize, host response varies from positive to negative depending on both the plant variety and the AMF species (Watts‐Williams et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a specific finding about sorghum supported by citation.

claim: Host response is typically measured in young plants grown under controlled conditions.
source: However, host response is typically measured in young plants grown under controlled conditions, and the values obtained may under-estimate the true importance of AM symbiosis in the field.
evidence: This is a statement about common experimental practices and their limitations.

claim: Host response values obtained from young plants under controlled conditions may under-estimate the true importance of AM symbiosis in the field.
source: However, host response is typically measured in young plants grown under controlled conditions, and the values obtained may under-estimate the true importance of AM symbiosis in the field.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of controlled experiments.

claim: It is important to distinguish inbred lines from hybrids and open-pollinated landrace varieties used in cultivation when considering maize response to AMF.
source: In the specific case of maize, it is important to distinguish the inbred lines characterized in most published reports from the hybrids and open-pollinated landrace varieties used in cultivation (c.f. other major cereal crops that are naturally inbreeding).
evidence: This is a reasoning-based statement about experimental design considerations.

claim: Heterosis ('hybrid vigor') will tend to reduce dependence and, consequently, host response to AMF.
source: Heterosis ('hybrid vigor') will tend to reduce dependence and, consequently, host response to AMF.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of heterosis on AMF response.

claim: Reduced proportional response to AMF in hybrids does not imply that arbuscular mycorrhizae are unimportant in hybrid maize cultivation.
source: This does not imply that arbuscular mycorrhizae are unimportant in hybrid maize cultivation, only that proportional responses may differ with the degree of inbreeding.
evidence: This is a clarification about the interpretation of response differences.

claim: The F2:3 families are segregating over approximately 50% of the genome, with any given individual retaining approximately 25% heterozygosity.
source: Our F2:3 families are segregating over ~50% of the genome, any given individual retaining ~25% heterozygosity.
evidence: This is a description of the genetic composition of the experimental material.

claim: The F2:3 material is intermediate between an F1 hybrid and an inbred line in terms of heterozygosity.
source: As such, this material is intermediate between an F1 hybrid and an inbred line.
evidence: This is an inference about the genetic nature of the experimental material.

claim: Introgression of the castor mutation into different genetic backgrounds will allow the generation of AMF-R hybrids and subsequent evaluation of their performance in field trials.
source: Introgression of the castor mutation into different genetic backgrounds will allow the generation of AMF-R hybrids and subsequent evaluation of their performance in field trials.
evidence: This is a proposed future application of the castor mutation.

claim: The approach might be applied readily to other crops provided suitable mutants are available.
source: More generally, our approach might be applied readily to other crops provided suitable mutants are available.
evidence: This is a proposed extension of the methodology to other species.

claim: There is substantial evidence for differences in host response among plant genotypes.
source: We found evidence for substantial differences in host response among plant genotypes.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the genetic analysis.

claim: In terms of variance explained, AMF × QTL effects were more important than the QTL main effects for total kernel weight, total kernel number, and fifty-kernel weight.
source: In terms of variance explained, AMF × QTL effects were more important than the QTL main effects for total kernel weight, total kernel number, and fifty-kernel weight.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from variance partitioning analysis.

claim: There is no evidence that the W22 and CML312 parents, as 'modern' inbred lines, had lost the capacity to benefit from AM symbiosis.
source: We saw no evidence that our W22 and CML312 parents, as 'modern' inbred lines, had lost the capacity to benefit from AM symbiosis (e.g. see Koide et al., 1988; Hetrick et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data, with reference to previous hypotheses in the literature.

claim: The identification of QTL linked to benefit suggests that it would be possible to improve the capacity of plants to profit from the symbiosis by combining positive alleles.
source: Furthermore, the identification of QTL linked to benefit suggests that it would be possible to improve the capacity of plants to profit from the symbiosis by combining positive alleles.
evidence: This is an inference about breeding applications based on the QTL findings.

claim: Additional characterization is required to discover the mechanistic basis of the differences in host response.
source: Additional characterization is required to discover the mechanistic basis of the differences we saw in the host response.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: A greater abundance of root internal fungal structures is not necessarily an indicator of greater host response.
source: Although we have yet to conduct a detailed quantification of colonization across all families, a greater abundance of root internal fungal structures is not necessarily an indicator of greater host response (Kaeppler et al., 2000; Sawers et al., 2017; Watts‐Williams et al., 2019; Plouznikoff et al., 2019; Pawlowski et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a general statement about the relationship between colonization and response, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The capacity of the host to limit fungal colonization under certain conditions may maximize plant benefit.
source: Indeed, the capacity of the host to limit fungal colonization under certain conditions may maximize plant benefit, and plants will restrict colonization under high nutrient conditions (Karlo et al., 2020; Nouri et al., 2014; Sawers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about host regulation of symbiosis supported by citations.

claim: Plants will restrict AMF colonization under high nutrient conditions.
source: Indeed, the capacity of the host to limit fungal colonization under certain conditions may maximize plant benefit, and plants will restrict colonization under high nutrient conditions (Karlo et al., 2020; Nouri et al., 2014; Sawers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a known phenomenon in plant-AMF interactions supported by citations.

claim: It has been proposed that the absence of the high-colonization allele of OsCERK1 from japonica rice reflects the action of human selection.
source: It has been proposed that the absence of the high-colonization allele of OsCERK1 from japonica rice reflects the action of human selection (Huang et al., 2020), consistent with the idea that greater colonization may not always beneficial.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citation.

claim: The extent of the external hyphal network may be more significant than the level of root colonization in terms of nutrient foraging.
source: In terms of nutrient foraging, the extent of the external hyphal network may be more significant than the level of root colonization (Yao et al., 2001; Munkvold et al., 2004; Schnepf et al., 2008; Sawers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about AMF function supported by citations.

claim: Many factors will interact to determine the symbiotic outcome.
source: Overall, many factors will interact to determine the symbiotic outcome.
evidence: This is a general statement about the complexity of the symbiosis.

claim: Certain bacterial taxa exert beneficial and synergistic effects on AM symbiosis, acting as 'mycorrhiza helpers'.
source: It has been shown that certain bacterial taxa exert beneficial and synergistic effects on AM symbiosis, acting as so-called 'mycorrhiza helpers' (Frey-Klett et al., 2007; van der Heijden et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about microbial interactions supported by citations.

claim: In Lotus japonicus, disruption of the AM symbiosis impacts other members of the root-associated microbial community.
source: In Lotus japonicus, disruption of the AM symbiosis impacts other members of the root-associated microbial community (Xue et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a specific finding from another species supported by citation.

claim: Characterization of the root microbiome of AMF-S and AMF-R families will provide insight into the interplay between AMF, the broader microbial community, and host response.
source: Characterization of the root microbiome of AMF-S and AMF-R families will provide insight into the interplay between AMF, the broader microbial community, and host response.
evidence: This is a proposed future research direction.

claim: The analysis indicated a functional trade-off between host dependence and benefit.
source: Our analysis indicated a functional trade-off between host dependence and benefit: the genotypes predicted to be the best in AM susceptible families were predicted to be unremarkable or poor in the context of AM resistance, and vice versa.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the genomic prediction analysis.

claim: The genotypes predicted to be the best in AM susceptible families were predicted to be unremarkable or poor in the context of AM resistance, and vice versa.
source: Our analysis indicated a functional trade-off between host dependence and benefit: the genotypes predicted to be the best in AM susceptible families were predicted to be unremarkable or poor in the context of AM resistance, and vice versa.
evidence: This is a specific result from the genomic prediction analysis.

claim: Examples of antagonistic pleiotropy were seen for QTL associated with days-to-silking, ear weight, total kernel weight, number of kernels per row, and fifty kernel weight.
source: At the level of individual loci, examples of antagonistic pleiotropy (Des Marais and Juenger, 2010) were seen for QTL associated with days-to-silking, ear weight, total kernel weight, number of kernels per row, and fifty kernel weight.
evidence: This is a summary of QTL analysis results.

claim: The identification of intraspecific genetic trade-offs is analogous to differences seen in plant nutritional strategy at higher taxonomic levels.
source: Our identification of intraspecific genetic trade-offs is analogous to differences seen in plant nutritional strategy at higher taxonomic levels, where the demands placed on plant anatomy and physiology by direct foraging or engagement in AM symbiosis appear to prevent co-optimization for both (Lambers et al., 2008; Wen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison to broader evolutionary patterns supported by citations.

claim: The demands placed on plant anatomy and physiology by direct foraging or engagement in AM symbiosis appear to prevent co-optimization for both strategies.
source: Our identification of intraspecific genetic trade-offs is analogous to differences seen in plant nutritional strategy at higher taxonomic levels, where the demands placed on plant anatomy and physiology by direct foraging or engagement in AM symbiosis appear to prevent co-optimization for both (Lambers et al., 2008; Wen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a general principle from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Increasing the proportion of root cortical aerenchyma reduces the carbon demand of the root system, promoting foraging efficiency.
source: For example, increasing the proportion of root cortical aerenchyma (root air space) reduces the carbon demand of the root system, promoting foraging efficiency (Postma and Lynch, 2011), but at the cost of limiting colonization by AMF and, potentially, host response (Strock et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a specific example of a trade-off supported by citation.

claim: Increasing root cortical aerenchyma limits colonization by AMF and, potentially, host response.
source: For example, increasing the proportion of root cortical aerenchyma (root air space) reduces the carbon demand of the root system, promoting foraging efficiency (Postma and Lynch, 2011), but at the cost of limiting colonization by AMF and, potentially, host response (Strock et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a specific finding about root anatomy and AMF supported by citation.

claim: It was somewhat surprising to see a QTL for tassel branch number to be conditional on susceptibility to AMF.
source: It was somewhat surprising to see a QTL for a morphological trait such as tassel branch number to be conditional on susceptibility to AMF, indicative of the action of pleiotropic systemic signals.
evidence: This is a comment on an unexpected finding from the QTL analysis.

claim: A QTL for tassel branch number being conditional on susceptibility to AMF is indicative of the action of pleiotropic systemic signals.
source: It was somewhat surprising to see a QTL for a morphological trait such as tassel branch number to be conditional on susceptibility to AMF, indicative of the action of pleiotropic systemic signals.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the QTL effect.

claim: The same phytohormones that play a key role in plant development are also implicated in the establishment and regulation of AM symbiosis.
source: Indeed, the same phytohormones that play a key role in plant development (including patterning of tassel architecture) are also implicated in the establishment and regulation of AM symbiosis (Gutjahr, 2014; Bonfante and Genre, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about hormone signaling supported by citations.

claim: The disruption of ethylene signaling has been shown to modulate the level of (negative) host response to AMF in Nicotiana attenuata.
source: For example, the disruption of ethylene signaling has been shown to modulate the level of (negative) host response to AMF in Nicotiana attenuata (Riedel et al., 2008); a DELLA repressor in the gibberellic acid signaling pathway is essential for colonization by AMF in rice ( Yu et al., 2014); a feedback-loop involving strigolactone modulates the extent of colonization by AMF in Medicago truncatula (Müller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a specific example from the literature supported by citation.

claim: A DELLA repressor in the gibberellic acid signaling pathway is essential for colonization by AMF in rice.
source: For example, the disruption of ethylene signaling has been shown to modulate the level of (negative) host response to AMF in Nicotiana attenuata (Riedel et al., 2008); a DELLA repressor in the gibberellic acid signaling pathway is essential for colonization by AMF in rice ( Yu et al., 2014); a feedback-loop involving strigolactone modulates the extent of colonization by AMF in Medicago truncatula (Müller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a specific finding from rice supported by citation.

claim: A feedback-loop involving strigolactone modulates the extent of colonization by AMF in Medicago truncatula.
source: For example, the disruption of ethylene signaling has been shown to modulate the level of (negative) host response to AMF in Nicotiana attenuata (Riedel et al., 2008); a DELLA repressor in the gibberellic acid signaling pathway is essential for colonization by AMF in rice ( Yu et al., 2014); a feedback-loop involving strigolactone modulates the extent of colonization by AMF in Medicago truncatula (Müller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a specific finding from Medicago supported by citation.

claim: It may be significant that many of the phytohormone signals involved in AM symbiosis have been the targets of domestication and plant improvement.
source: It may be significant that many of these same signals have been the targets of domestication and plant improvement (Sawers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative connection to breeding history supported by citation.

claim: QTL × AMF effects were in many cases driven by plasticity associated with the temperate W22 allele.
source: QTL × AMF effects were in many cases driven by plasticity associated with the temperate W22 allele; that is, effects linked to alleles from the better adapted sub-tropical CML312 parent were more stable with respect to the presence or absence of AMF in our sub-tropical field.
evidence: This is an observation from the QTL analysis.

claim: Effects linked to alleles from the better adapted sub-tropical CML312 parent were more stable with respect to the presence or absence of AMF in the sub-tropical field.
source: QTL × AMF effects were in many cases driven by plasticity associated with the temperate W22 allele; that is, effects linked to alleles from the better adapted sub-tropical CML312 parent were more stable with respect to the presence or absence of AMF in our sub-tropical field.
evidence: This is an observation from the QTL analysis.

claim: The result might be interpreted as evidence of the AM symbiosis mitigating or buffering the deleterious effect of 'non-native' W22 alleles.
source: This same result might be interpreted as evidence of the AM symbiosis mitigating or buffering the deleterious effect of 'non-native' W22 alleles.
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation of the QTL patterns.

claim: It will be interesting to characterize additional host genotypes, including those considered to be more responsive to AMF and landrace and wild-relative diversity.
source: It will be interesting to characterize additional host genotypes, including those considered to be more responsive to AMF (e.g. Sawers et al., 2017) and landrace and wild-relative diversity.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: It has been suggested that mutualisms play a role during adaptation to new or stressful environments.
source: It has been suggested that mutalisms play a role during adaptation to new or stressful environments (O'Brien et al., 2018; O'Brien et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations.

claim: The genetic architecture observed implies a role for AMF in influencing yield stability in addition to affecting yield.
source: In addition to affecting yield, the genetic architecture we observed implies a role for AMF in influencing yield stability.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic architecture findings.

claim: Given the unpredictability in the AM community across location or year, optimization of the plant host might require consistency of response as much as maximum benefit.
source: Given the unpredictability in the AM community across location or year, optimization of the plant host might require consistency of response as much as maximum benefit.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about breeding objectives.

claim: There is no evidence of selective pressures to reduce colonization by AMF in maize breeding.
source: Although we have found no evidence of selective pressures to reduce colonization by AMF in maize breeding, the trade-offs we describe suggest that efforts to optimize plants for better performance either with or without the contribution of microorganisms may not be easily aligned.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study findings.

claim: The trade-offs described suggest that efforts to optimize plants for better performance either with or without the contribution of microorganisms may not be easily aligned.
source: Although we have found no evidence of selective pressures to reduce colonization by AMF in maize breeding, the trade-offs we describe suggest that efforts to optimize plants for better performance either with or without the contribution of microorganisms may not be easily aligned.
evidence: This is an inference about breeding implications based on the trade-off findings.

claim: We may need to make decisions about the types of agroecosystems we want and develop our crops accordingly.
source: Ultimately, we may need to make decisions about the types of agroecosystems we want and develop our crops accordingly.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future agricultural development.
